title: Ising superconductivity and anomalous metallic states in a bulk crystal with artificial unidirectional stacking layers
comment: main text 19 pages (4 figures) and SI 15 pages (11 figures)
summary: The two-dimensional (2D) limit in macroscopic bulk crystals provides a powerful platform for exploring exotic quantum phases. Here, we report the synthesis of a Sr0.75ClNbS2 superconductor that achieves unidirectional, parallel AA stacking-a configuration never before realized in a bulk crystal. Unlike conventional intercalation, which merely expands the interlayer spacing, our approach employs a planar Sr-Cl network to enforce a complete stacking reorganization, driving all NbS2 layers from the native antiparallel AB stacking into a unidirectional, parallel AA arrangement. This stacking switch globally breaks inversion symmetry, transforming centrosymmetric 2H-NbS2 into a noncentrosymmetric bulk crystal with D3h point group symmetry. Crucially, this structural design reproduces, in three dimensions, the electronic environment of an isolated monolayer, thereby preventing cancellation of the local Ising fields. As a result, strong Ising spin-orbit coupling and spin-split bands persist throughout the bulk. Transport measurements reveal extreme superconducting anisotropy (γ ~ 77), an in-plane upper critical field (~ 10.65 T) that far exceeds the Pauli paramagnetic limit, and clean-limit superconductivity indicative of high crystalline quality. Moreover, magnetotransport uncovers a novel magnetic-field-induced anomalous metallic state characterized by finite dissipation yet a vanishing Hall response. Direct band-structure measurements corroborate the layer-decoupled, quasi-2D electronic nature of the system. This work establishes stacking-geometry engineering as a powerful strategy to artificially enforce a globally noncentrosymmetric, quasi-2D superconducting state in bulk crystals, paving the way for designing quantum materials with tunable crystalline symmetry and electronic band topology.

AI.tldr: Synthesis of Sr0.75ClNbS2 yields a bulk crystal with enforced unidirectional AA stacking via a planar Sr–Cl network, converting centrosymmetric 2H‑NbS2 into a globally noncentrosymmetric, quasi‑2D superconductor that preserves monolayer-like Ising SOC and spin‑split bands. The material shows extreme superconducting anisotropy (γ≈77), an in‑plane Hc2 greatly exceeding the Pauli limit, clean‑limit transport, and a novel field‑induced anomalous metallic state with finite dissipation but zero Hall response; ARPES-like band measurements confirm layer‑decoupled quasi‑2D electronic structure.
AI.method: Materials synthesis by intercalation/stacking‑geometry engineering using a planar Sr–Cl network to force AA stacking; combined structural characterization, transport and magnetotransport measurements, and direct band‑structure probes (spectroscopic measurements) to establish electronic and superconducting properties.
AI.tags: superconductivity, noncentrosymmetric, Ising_spin-orbit, quasi-2D, stacking_engineering, topology, quantum_devices

title: Disorder-induced superconductivity in graphene
summary: Correlated phases of matter are typically investigated in crystalline systems, where disorder is considered to be detrimental. However, intriguing exceptions exist, such as superconductivity being enhanced in amorphous realizations of Al and Bi. Here, we demonstrate that superconductivity can even emerge entirely from disorder, using monolayer graphene as an example. In the clean limit, the semi-metallic nature of graphene requires prohibitively strong electronic interactions to achieve superconductivity. Despite the inherently random nature of disorder, we show that introducing low concentrations of vacancies or hydrogenation in graphene provides a large density of low-energy states that easily induce superconductivity. For conventional $s$-wave pairing, disorder induces a finite superconducting order parameter for arbitrarily weak attractive interactions. Rather than forming isolated superconducting puddles, global phase coherence is established through a finite superfluid weight of purely geometrical origin. Away from the chiral limit of vacancies, hydrogenation similarly yields a finite transition temperature and nonzero superfluid weight for weak interactions. For unconventional nearest-neighbor pairing, typically more disrupted by disorder, superconductivity exhibits quantum-critical-like behavior, yet phase coherence persists at low interaction strengths, with mixed $d$-wave symmetries. Our work demonstrates the robust emergence of macroscopic superconducting phase coherence engineered entirely from microscopic disorder.

AI.tldr: Disorder (vacancies or hydrogenation) in monolayer graphene creates a large density of low-energy states that can induce macroscopic superconductivity even for arbitrarily weak attractive interactions. For conventional s‑wave pairing this yields a finite superconducting order parameter and a global phase-coherent state supported by a nonzero superfluid weight of geometric origin; for nearest‑neighbor (unconventional) pairing superconductivity shows quantum‑critical‑like behavior with mixed d‑wave symmetry but retains phase coherence at weak coupling.
AI.method: The study models monolayer graphene with low concentrations of vacancies or hydrogenation and analyzes the resulting low‑energy density of states and superconducting response for both on‑site (s‑wave) and nearest‑neighbor (unconventional) pairing channels. Key diagnostics are the emergence of a finite order parameter, transition temperature, and a nonzero superfluid weight (notably of geometric origin), including consideration of the chiral vacancy limit and symmetry of the gap (mixed d‑wave) in the unconventional case.
AI.tags: quantum_geometry, superconducting_impurity, graphene, disorder, s-wave, d-wave, vacancies, hydrogenation, phase_coherence, quantum_critical

title: Fabrication of high-quality topological insulator nanodevices from bulk-insulating air-sensitive Sb-Bi$_2$Se$_3$
comment: 20 pages total; 9 pages main text with 5 figures and 11 pages of supplement with 8 figures
summary: High-quality topological insulator (TI) materials are essential for the realization and detection of Majorana bound states (MBSs) in TI-superconductor hybrid platforms. Widely used compensated TIs exhibit substantial disorder and charge inhomogeneity, which may be detrimental for Majorana devices. In this regard, Sb-substituted Bi$_2$Se$_3$ (SBS) is promising, because it is non-compensated and yet achieves very low bulk carrier density. We systematically investigate the impact of thermal processing during microfabrication on the transport properties of SBS. We developed a room-temperature fabrication protocol that preserves the low carrier density of exfoliated SBS upon fabrication of Hall bar and nanowire devices as evidenced from the observation of quantum interference oscillations in nanowires, a large gate tunability, and clear signatures of weak antilocalization (WAL).

AI.tldr: Sb-substituted Bi2Se3 (SBS) is demonstrated as a low-bulk-carrier-density topological-insulator platform compatible with device fabrication: a room-temperature microfabrication protocol preserves the low carrier density of exfoliated SBS, yielding Hall-bar and nanowire devices that show quantum-interference oscillations, large gate tunability, and clear weak-antilocalization signatures.
AI.method: Systematic study of the effect of thermal processing during microfabrication; development and application of a room-temperature fabrication protocol for exfoliated SBS followed by transport characterization (Hall measurements, gate dependence, and magnetotransport revealing quantum interference oscillations and weak antilocalization in nanowires).

title: Resonant cooling of nuclear spins by optically-oriented holes in MAPbI$_3$ perovskite crystals
summary: Resonant cooling of nuclear spins by photogenerated spin-oriented holes is demonstrated for MAPbI$_3$ perovskite crystals. It is evidenced by Hanle-effect measurements under helicity-modulated excitation with variable frequency. The resonance position in magnetic field shifts toward higher fields with increasing modulation frequency. The invariance of the Hanle curve upon in-plane sample rotation is consistent with the involvement of $^{207}$Pb nuclei with spin $I = 1/2$, which do not exhibit quadrupolar splitting. The shape of the resonance feature in the Hanle curve reveals that the nuclear spins are cooled by carriers with a negative $g$-factor, consistent with holes. The resonance fields associated with the modulation frequencies exceed the half-width of the weakly localized hole contribution to the Hanle curve, indicating that strongly localized holes are the primary carriers responsible for the nuclear spin cooling.

AI.tldr: Resonant cooling of nuclear spins in MAPbI3 perovskite crystals is demonstrated via helicity‑modulated optical pumping: Hanle‑effect measurements show frequency-dependent resonance fields attributed to 207Pb (I=1/2) nuclei and indicate that strongly localized holes (negative g‑factor) are responsible for the nuclear spin cooling.
AI.method: Frequency‑resolved Hanle‑effect measurements under helicity‑modulated optical excitation; analysis of Hanle‑curve shape, in‑plane rotation invariance, resonance position vs modulation frequency, and comparison of resonance fields to the Hanle half‑width to infer involvement of 207Pb nuclei and strongly localized holes.
AI.tags: perovskite, nuclear_spin_cooling, Hanle_effect, optical_pumping, spintronics, 207Pb, localized_holes, quantum_devices

title: Quantum Heat Under the Microscope: A Perspective on Cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy
summary: Exploring thermal transport at cryogenic temperatures presents both significant challenges and valuable insights. By uncovering the thermal counterpart of well-known quantum phenomena, researchers investigated fascinating phenomena ranging from the violation of the Wiedemann-Franz law to the quantisation of phonons. One key frontier remains : no existing method can image local heat transport at the nanoscale under cryogenic conditions. In this Perspective, we review the current state state of the art of local heat transport characterisation techniques and highlight their limitations. As a motivation for the development of cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy, we provide five case studies illustrating how this approach could deepen our understanding of exotic quantum phases and enable the emergence of transformative technologies.

AI.tldr: Perspective review identifying the lack of any method to image local heat transport at the nanoscale under cryogenic conditions; surveys existing local heat-transport characterization techniques, highlights their limitations, and motivates development of cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy (cryo-SThM) via five case studies that connect nanoscale thermal imaging to phenomena such as Wiedemann–Franz law violations, phonon quantisation, and exotic quantum phases with potential technological impact.
AI.method: Critical literature review and perspective: assessment of current local thermal-transport techniques at cryogenic temperatures, identification of gaps, and proposal/advocacy for cryogenic Scanning Thermal Microscopy supported by five illustrative case studies.
AI.tags: thermal_transport, cryogenic_scanning_thermal_microscopy, nanoscale_imaging, Wiedemann–Franz_law, phonon_quantisation, exotic_quantum_phases, quantum_devices

title: An efficient formalism for inertial spin waves: Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya antiferromagnets as case studies
summary: Magnetic inertia, emerging in the ultrafast regime, supports inertial spin waves (SWs) as novel magnetic excitations. Despite considerable efforts devoted to inertial SWs, a systematic formalism for fully characterizing their intrinsic properties, especially chirality and polarization, is still lacking, and inertial SWs in spatially nonuniform magnetic configurations remain poorly explored. Here, we develop a framework for calculating inertial SWs and establish a general definition of their chirality and polarization via the ellipticity angle, a unified parameter encoding frequency sign, phase difference, and elliptical axis ratio. Using this method, we systematically investigate precessional and nutational SWs in uniaxial antiferromagnets with staggered and homogeneous Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMIs), covering uniform collinear, canted, and spiral magnetic configurations. The results reveal that small staggered DMI preserves spin-wave degeneracy, whereas small homogeneous DMI lifts it. Further space-time inversion symmetry breaking in canted and spiral structures fully removes spin-wave degeneracy across the entire Brillouin zone. Long-wavelength nutational SWs behave as backward waves, and flat bands emerge in canted and spiral configurations near a critical inertial relaxation time. In canted and spiral configurations, nutational modes are always lefthanded whereas precessional modes are always righthanded; additionally, the dispersion spectra of the canted configuration can be derived from those of the spiral configuration via band folding. Polarization is wavenumber insensitive for uniform configurations but becomes strongly dispersive for nonuniform ones. This work advances the fundamental understanding of magnetic inertial dynamics and provides theoretical insights for the development of ultrafast magnonic devices.

AI.tldr: Develops a unified formalism to compute and characterize inertial spin waves (precessional and nutational) via an ellipticity angle that encodes frequency sign, phase difference and elliptical axis ratio; applies this to uniaxial antiferromagnets with staggered and homogeneous Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction across uniform, canted and spiral textures, reporting degeneracy lifting by homogeneous DMI and symmetry breaking, backward-propagating long-wavelength nutational modes, emergent flat bands near a critical inertial relaxation time, and mode-specific handedness (nutational left, precessional right).
AI.method: Constructs a linearized spin-wave framework that incorporates magnetic inertia and defines chirality/polarization through a single ellipticity-angle parameter; uses this formalism to calculate dispersions, polarization/ellipticity and symmetry-driven degeneracy (including band folding relations) for model uniaxial antiferromagnets with staggered/homogeneous DMI in uniform, canted and spiral ground states.
AI.tags: magnetic_inertia, inertial_spin_waves, antiferromagnet, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya, spin-wave_polarization, magnonics, chirality, band_structure

title: Anisotropic tunneling through magnetic barriers in 8-Pmmn borophene
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures. Version to appear in Phys. Lett. A 2026
summary: We present a theoretical study of electron tunneling through a magnetic barrier in 8-Pmmn borophene, created by depositing two ferromagnetic strips on the borophene sheet. Using a low-energy effective Hamiltonian that captures the anisotropic Dirac spectrum, we solve the Dirac equation in three regions and impose wave-function continuity at the interfaces. From the resulting spinor solutions, we compute current densities and determine transmission and reflection probabilities as functions of incident energy, angle, and barrier parameters. The transmission exhibits strong anisotropy due to the tilted Dirac cones, with pronounced suppression for specific incident directions, suggesting directional filtering of carriers. We further calculate the conductance using the Landauer-Büttiker formalism, revealing that both magnetic strength and barrier width can tune the charge transport properties. The results demonstrate that engineered magnetic barriers in 8-Pmmn borophene enable precise control over electron flow, offering a platform for anisotropic transport control and tunable quantum devices. The interplay between the intrinsic anisotropy of borophene and external magnetic barriers provides rich opportunities to manipulate Dirac fermions in two-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically analyzes electron tunneling through a ferromagnetic-induced magnetic barrier in 8-Pmmn borophene. Using an anisotropic, tilted-Dirac low-energy model it finds strongly angle-dependent (directional) suppression of transmission and shows conductance can be tuned by barrier strength and width—proposing engineered magnetic barriers as a platform for anisotropic transport control and tunable 2D quantum devices.
AI.method: Construct low-energy effective Hamiltonian for anisotropic/tilted Dirac spectrum; solve the Dirac equation in three regions with wave-function continuity at interfaces to obtain spinor solutions; compute current densities to extract transmission/reflection as functions of incident energy, angle, and barrier parameters; evaluate conductance via the Landauer–Büttiker formalism.
AI.tags: 8-Pmmn borophene, anisotropic Dirac fermions, magnetic barrier, directional filtering, quantum_transport, Landauer-Büttiker, quantum_devices

title: The Wigner function for Integer quantum Hall effect
summary: Wigner's quasi-probability distribution function in phase space is a specialized representation of the density matrix, possessing significant physical importance. In this article, we first review the wave function describing electronic motion in an electromagnetic field under the Landau gauge. Next, based on an introduction to the properties of the Wigner function, we calculate the Wigner function for the integer quantum Hall effect using the integral method.

AI.tldr: Paper derives the Wigner quasi-probability distribution for electrons in the integer quantum Hall effect by evaluating the Wigner function of Landau-gauge wavefunctions; it also reviews the Landau-gauge electronic wavefunction and Wigner-function properties.
AI.method: Analytical calculation of the Wigner function via the integral representation (integral transform of the density matrix/wavefunction) using Landau-gauge single-particle wavefunctions for the integer quantum Hall effect.

title: Quantum-geometric shift of quasiequilibrium: Origin of nonreciprocal current driven by quantum-metric dipole
summary: We study nonlinear DC electric transport of quantum-metric origin by combining adiabatic perturbation theory with the nonequilibrium Green function approach. The adiabatic ansatz provides a basis for directly treating a DC electric field in the velocity gauge, rather than introducing it as the zero-frequency limit of an AC field. The resulting adiabatic-basis Hamiltonian takes the same form as in the length gauge, enabling a systematic comparison across different formulations. Applying this fully quantum formulation, we find a longitudinal nonreciprocal current governed by the quantum-metric dipole. The essential ingredient is a quantum correction to the distribution function that is absent in semiclassical treatments. We trace this correction to the finite spread of an electron wave packet during relaxation under a bias field, thereby identifying shifted quasiequilibrium as the physical origin of quantum-metric nonreciprocal transport.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a fully quantum treatment of nonlinear DC electric transport arising from the quantum metric: using an adiabatic ansatz in the velocity gauge combined with nonequilibrium Green functions, the authors identify a longitudinal nonreciprocal current governed by a quantum-metric dipole. The effect originates from a quantum correction to the distribution function (shifted quasiequilibrium) due to finite electron wave-packet spread during relaxation.
AI.method: Combine adiabatic perturbation theory (adiabatic ansatz for treating a DC electric field in the velocity gauge) with the nonequilibrium Green function formalism; derive an adiabatic-basis Hamiltonian equivalent to the length gauge and compute quantum corrections to the distribution leading to a quantum-metric-driven nonreciprocal DC current.

title: A 2048-spin bulk acoustic wave Ising machine for number partitioning and Sudoku
summary: Optical coherent Ising machines based on time-multiplexing have demonstrated significant progress in terms of connectivity and spin scalability. However, they are constrained by large physical footprints, high power consumption, poor thermal stability, and high cost. Here, we present a time-multiplexed Ising machine leveraging propagating wave packets in solid-state delay lines at microwave frequencies, enabling thermally stable, robust, low-power, tabletop, and affordable design. We use two serially connected 20.5 MHz, 707 μs bulk acoustic wave delay lines supporting 2,048 spins. Our design provides all-to-all connectivity with 15-bit coupling resolution and finds approximate MAX-CUT solutions in 341 ms, potentially scalable to sub-ms by using higher frequency delay lines. Additionally, we demonstrate solutions to number partitioning and Sudoku problems. Compared with state-of-the-art Coherent Ising machines, our machine exhibits four orders of magnitude higher thermal stability. Against the simulated bifurcation algorithm, our design achieves comparable results on the MAX-CUT problem, while outperforming it on the more complex number-partitioning and Sudoku problems.

AI.tldr: Time-multiplexed Ising machine implemented with propagating microwave wave packets in solid-state bulk-acoustic-wave delay lines: two serial 20.5 MHz, 707 μs delay lines realize 2,048 spins with all-to-all coupling (15-bit resolution), solving MAX-CUT in 341 ms and demonstrating number-partitioning and Sudoku; thermally stable (×10^4 improvement) and potentially sub-ms with higher-frequency delay lines.
AI.method: Hardware implementation of a coherent Ising-machine architecture using time-multiplexing of propagating wave packets in solid-state bulk acoustic wave (BAW) microwave delay lines (two serially connected 20.5 MHz, 707 μs delays) to realize 2,048 spins, 15-bit programmable all-to-all coupling; empirical benchmarking against MAX-CUT, number-partitioning and Sudoku instances and comparison to optical CIMs and a simulated bifurcation algorithm.
AI.tags: quantum_devices, Ising_machine, time-multiplexing, bulk_acoustic_wave, microwave_delay_lines, MAX-CUT, number_partitioning, Sudoku, thermal_stability

title: Electrical transport in ultra-thin films: from Fuchs-Sondheimer to quantum-confinement
summary: Ultra-thin films are fundamental components of modern nanoelectronics, where reducing thickness to the few-nanometer scale leads to a dramatic increase in electrical resistivity. For decades, this behavior has been interpreted in terms of classical size effects, primarily surface scattering within the Fuchs--Sondheimer theory and grain-boundary scattering in the Mayadas--Shatzkes model. While these approaches successfully describe transport when the film thickness is comparable to the electronic mean free path, growing experimental evidence indicates that they become insufficient under extreme confinement. This review discusses the crossover from classical scattering to a quantum-confinement regime in which the electronic states available for transport are fundamentally restructured by finite size. We review the recently proposed reciprocal-space confinement theory, which predicts an exponential increase of resistivity with decreasing thickness at the nanoscale, and discuss how it can be combined with classical surface-scattering models to provide a unified description of ultra-thin metallic and semiconducting films. Finally, we summarize recent experimental evidence supporting this picture and discuss its implications for future nanoelectronic devices, nanoscale interconnects, and quantum transport under extreme spatial confinement.

AI.tldr: Review argues that classical size-effect models (Fuchs–Sondheimer, Mayadas–Shatzkes) break down under extreme thickness confinement and presents the reciprocal-space confinement theory — which predicts an exponential rise of resistivity with decreasing thickness — together with a hybrid framework combining quantum-confinement and classical surface-scattering to describe ultra-thin metallic and semiconducting films; experimental evidence and device implications are surveyed.
AI.method: Literature review and theoretical synthesis: critical comparison of classical surface- and grain-scattering models with the recently proposed reciprocal-space confinement theory; formulation of a unified (hybrid) modeling approach that combines exponential quantum-confinement resistivity scaling with classical scattering, plus a summary of supporting experiments.

title: Entropy of Non-Abelian Anyons from Slow Quasiparticle Dynamics in Quantum Hall Interferometers
summary: Non-Abelian anyons emerging in fractional quantum Hall states carry a characteristic entropy, $ΔS = k_B \log d$, where \(d\) is the anyon's quantum dimension. This \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) entropy can, in principle, be extracted from charge measurements of an antidot via Maxwell relations. However, equilibrium charge measurements in fractional antidots have proven to be challenging with conventional charge detectors. Here, we propose a scheme based on an antidot embedded in an interferometer, in which the charge can be inferred from the recently observed time-dependent switching of the interference phase. Performing such non-local charge measurements at equilibrium, the characteristic \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) entropy of non-Abelian anyons (e.g., $d = \sqrt{2}$ for the $ν= 5/2$ state) can be extracted for intermediate temperatures, which exceed the level spacing of the interferometer edge, but are much smaller than the level spacing of the antidot.

AI.tldr: Proposes extracting the O(1) entropy ΔS = k_B log d of non‑Abelian anyons in fractional quantum Hall antidots by inferring antidot charge from time-dependent switching of an interferometer’s interference phase; using Maxwell relations at equilibrium and an intermediate temperature window (above interferometer-edge level spacing, below antidot level spacing) allows direct measurement of the anyon quantum dimension (e.g. d=√2 at ν=5/2).
AI.method: Embed the antidot inside an electronic interferometer and infer its equilibrium charge non‑locally from recently observed time-dependent phase switching of interference; apply Maxwell relations to convert measured charge variations into entropy, using an intermediate temperature regime where edge level spacings are thermally smeared but antidot level spacing remains discrete.

title: Josephson and Spin Currents in Coupled Polariton Condensates
summary: We analyze particle and spin currents in networks of coupled spinor exciton-polariton condensates arranged as plaquettes and regular polygonal rings. In closed geometries, spin-conserving and TE-TM-induced spin-flip tunnelling combine to generate circulating particle currents, hidden spin counterflows, and bond-dependent spin-current patterns. For the minimal geometries - an equilateral triangle, and a square plaquette - we derive analytical expressions for edge-resolved currents from stationary configurations obtained by energy minimization. We then show how particle, in-plane spin, and out-of-plane spin currents partition the parameter plane and provide direct signatures of the equilibrium phases. Finally, we apply the same current-resolved diagnostics to larger rings, where winding numbers and a branch-invariant common-phase coherence metric organize the resulting phase structure.

AI.tldr: Networks of spinor exciton-polariton condensates on small plaquettes and polygonal rings support circulating particle currents, bond-dependent spin-current patterns and hidden spin counterflows driven by spin-conserving and TE–TM-induced spin-flip tunnelling. For triangle and square units the authors derive analytical edge-resolved currents from stationary states found via energy minimization; particle, in-plane and out-of-plane spin currents then partition parameter space and diagnose equilibrium phases. The same current-resolved diagnostics are applied to larger rings where winding numbers and a branch-invariant common-phase coherence metric organize the phase structure.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of edge-resolved currents from stationary configurations obtained by energy minimization for minimal geometries (triangle, square); construction of current-resolved diagnostics (particle, in-plane spin, out-of-plane spin) to map equilibrium phases; extension of these diagnostics to larger polygonal rings characterized by winding numbers and a branch-invariant common-phase coherence metric.
AI.tags: topology, quantum_devices, exciton_polaritons, spin_currents, TE-TM_coupling, plaquettes, energy_minimization, polygonal_rings

title: Coupled Spin-Orbital $p$-Wave Magnetism via Structural and Magnetic Chirality
summary: Helical spin textures represent the minimal realization of $p$-wave magnetism which is characterized by momentum-odd spin polarization. Independently, structurally chiral crystals exhibit momentum-odd orbital polarization arising from broken inversion symmetry. Here, we demonstrate that spin-orbit coupling couples these two independent microscopic chirality degrees of freedom, allowing the orbital polarization of a chiral crystal to generate an additional contribution to the $p$-wave spin splitting. The resulting spin-orbital state is naturally classified by the relative chirality $η=χ_{\mathrm c}χ_{\mathrm m}$, giving rise to two symmetry-distinct $p$-wave phases corresponding to homochiral and heterochiral configurations which can be directly probed by the longitudinal conductivity. These phases exhibit distinct transport signatures, establishing relative chirality as an experimentally accessible symmetry degree of freedom in chiral magnetic systems.

AI.tldr: Spin-orbit coupling in chiral crystals links momentum-odd orbital polarization to helical (p-wave) spin textures, producing an extra p-wave spin splitting. The combined spin–orbital state is classified by the relative chirality η=χ_c χ_m into homochiral and heterochiral p-wave phases that have distinct longitudinal-conductivity signatures, making relative chirality an experimentally accessible symmetry degree of freedom.
AI.method: Analytical, symmetry-based theoretical analysis of spin–orbit coupling between orbital and spin chirality; classification of resulting spin–orbital states via the relative chirality η and prediction of distinct transport (longitudinal conductivity) signatures for the two symmetry-distinct p-wave phases.
AI.tags: p-wave_magnetism, spin-orbit_coupling, chiral_crystals, orbital_polarization, magnetic_chirality, transport_signatures

title: Intrinsic orbital Hall effect in a nonuniform electric field
summary: Geometric analysis of electronic Bloch states offers a universal framework for understanding electronic properties, yet its role in the transport of orbital angular momentum remains unexplored. In this work, we establish an analytic connection between orbital angular momentum transport and the geometric properties of Bloch wave functions in electronic systems. Focusing on the intrinsic orbital Hall effect in the dc limit under a spatially nonuniform electric field, we show that its conductivity can be expressed in terms of universal geometric quantities, such as the orbital Berry curvature and quantum metric. This formulation provides a term-by-term correspondence with the geometric description of intrinsic charge Hall transport established in previous studies. Using a tight-binding model, we further illustrate that the higher-order orbital Hall response can exhibit enhanced sensitivity to the orientation of an anisotropic sample. Our work deepens the understanding of diverse intrinsic transverse transport phenomena and the role of quantum geometry in electronic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an analytic link between intrinsic orbital angular momentum transport (orbital Hall effect) and the quantum geometry of Bloch states, showing dc orbital Hall conductivity under a spatially nonuniform electric field can be written in terms of orbital Berry curvature and the quantum metric; a tight-binding example shows higher-order responses are sensitive to sample orientation.
AI.method: Analytic geometric formulation of intrinsic orbital Hall transport for Bloch electrons in the dc, spatially nonuniform-E-field limit, expressing conductivity in universal geometric quantities (orbital Berry curvature, quantum metric) with a termwise correspondence to known geometric descriptions of charge Hall transport; illustrated with a tight-binding model to demonstrate orientation-dependent higher-order response.
AI.tags: quantum_geometry, topology, orbital_Hall, Berry_curvature, quantum_metric, tight_binding, transverse_transport
